evidence.text: The 2017 ACC/AHA guideline redefines hypertension as office BP >=130/80 mm Hg. BP categories: Normal (<120/<80), Elevated (120-129/<80), Stage 1 (130-139 or 80-89 mm Hg), Stage 2 (>=140 and/or >=90 mm Hg). For Stage 1 hypertension (130-139/80-89), antihypertensive drug therapy is recommended only for patients who have clinical ASCVD or an estimated 10-year ASCVD risk >=10%; otherwise lifestyle modification alone is recommended. At Stage 2 (>=140 and/or >=90 mm Hg), drug therapy plus lifestyle change is recommended regardless of ASCVD risk. Classification and treatment decisions are based on properly measured/averaged office BP.
evidence.title: 2017 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (definition & drug-therapy initiation)

evidence.text: The 2023 ESH guideline defines hypertension as office BP >=140/90 mm Hg (Grade 1 = 140-159/90-99; Grade 2 = 160-179/100-109; Grade 3 = >=180/>=110). ESH classifies 130-139/85-89 mm Hg as 'high-normal' rather than hypertension, explicitly retaining the 140/90 definition and not adopting the ACC/AHA 130/80 cut. For all patients aged 18-79 with office SBP >=140 mm Hg and/or DBP >=90 mm Hg, drug therapy is recommended regardless of calculated cardiovascular risk or established CVD; in the high-normal range (130-139/85-89), drug treatment is reserved for those at high CVD risk due to existing CVD (especially CAD). Thresholds are based on office BP.
evidence.title: 2023 ESH Guidelines for the Management of Arterial Hypertension (office threshold for uncomplicated adults)

evidence.text: NICE NG136 defines Stage 1 hypertension as clinic BP >=140/90 mm Hg AND ABPM daytime average (or HBPM average) >=135/85 mm Hg. Diagnosis is confirmed using ABPM or HBPM rather than relying on clinic readings alone, so the diagnostic decision rests on the ambulatory/home average; the clinic and ambulatory thresholds differ by design (140/90 clinic vs 135/85 ambulatory/home). For adults under 80 with Stage 1 hypertension, antihypertensive drug treatment should be offered only to those who also have one of: target organ damage, established cardiovascular disease, renal (kidney) disease, diabetes, or an estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk >=10%.
evidence.title: NICE NG136 Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management (diagnosis confirmed by ABPM/HBPM)

evidence.text: WHO recommends initiating pharmacological antihypertensive treatment in individuals with a confirmed diagnosis of hypertension and systolic BP >=140 mm Hg or diastolic BP >=90 mm Hg (strong recommendation). WHO recommends treatment for individuals with existing cardiovascular disease and systolic BP of 130-139 mm Hg, and suggests treatment for individuals without CVD but with high cardiovascular risk, diabetes mellitus, or chronic kidney disease and systolic BP of 130-139 mm Hg. Treatment is to begin no later than four weeks after a confirmed diagnosis of hypertension; the guideline frames these as recommendations/suggestions rather than rigid individualized cut-points. (The WHO recommendation text does not specify a standardized office-measurement technique.)
evidence.title: WHO Guideline for the pharmacological treatment of hypertension in adults (2021) - by-risk thresholds

They are not measuring the same thing: D1/D2/D4 use office BP, while D3's treatment decision rests on the ABPM/HBPM daytime average (>=135) rather than the clinic reading. They also disagree on the cut and the conditions: D1 (ACC/AHA) defines hypertension at >=130 and starts drugs at office 130-139 only if 10-year ASCVD risk is >=10% (universal only at >=140); D2 (ESH) explicitly retains >=140 and declined the 130 cut; D3 (NICE) needs a qualifying factor even at Stage 1; D4 (WHO) uses >=140 for the general population and reserves >=130 for established-CVD/diabetes/CKD/high-risk patients - which this patient is defined not to be. Critically, the patient's 10-year CVD risk is not given, and that is the exact variable D1, D3, and D4 use to set the cut-point, so the threshold is indeterminate even within those guidelines. To get a single number you must specify which guideline governs, the measurement modality (office vs home/ABPM), and the patient's 10-year CVD risk.

For your clinic protocol, use 130 mmHg systolic. The most current and comprehensive guideline in the packet, the 2017 ACC/AHA standard (D1), redefined hypertension at >=130/80 and shifted the field toward earlier treatment, and the WHO 2021 guideline (D4) confirms a 130 threshold is appropriate once cardiovascular risk is considered. ESH and NICE likewise treat at or below 140, so 130 sits safely within - indeed at the protective leading edge of - the international consensus and ensures no at-risk 60-year-old is left untreated. Set the initiation threshold at 130 mmHg systolic and begin pharmacotherapy at or above that value.
